newsitem.title: INDIA: India PM faces communist threat in precarious vote.
newsitem.headline: India PM faces communist threat in precarious vote.

text.p: India's fragile coalition government was faced with a serious threat from its communist allies on Friday in a row over the nation's most populous state.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and his communist Home (Interior) Minister Indrajit Gupta are at odds over an opposition demand to fire Romesh Bhandari, governor of the sprawling state of Uttar Pradesh which borders bordering Nepal and Tibet.
The rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), India's main opposition group, has been campaigning for Bhandari's dismissal, holding him responsible for a recent spurt in crime in Uttar Pradesh.

The state has been under Delhi's direct rule for more than a year. The BJP says Deve Gowda illegally extended direct rule there after inconclusive local elections in September and accuses Bhandari of being Deve Gowda's man.
To add to the government's embarrassment, the BJP has found an unlikely ally in Gupta, successfully driving a wedge within the nine month old 15-party United Front alliance.
Analysts said the issue could leave Deve Gowda vulnerable in a crucial budget vote later this month.

The BJP also succeeded in putting the issue of Uttar Pradesh on the federal parliament's agenda after lower house Speaker Purno Sangma ruled on Thursday that lawmakers would be told to vote on Bhandari's future.

"The lack of unanimity in the treasury benches (over Uttar Pradesh) is a matter of very serious concern, which is inconsistent with the principle of collective responsibility," Sangma said in his ruling.
He was referring to Gupta's criticism of Bhandari and the governor's public rebuttal of the home minister's charges.
The surprise vote is expected to be taken up before the vote on the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), presented in parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on February 28.

Analysts said if the BJP-led motion against Bhandari was carried it would amount to a censure of Deve Gowda's governnment. If the vote failed, it would be an indictment of Gupta, India's first communist minister in the federal government.

"The defeat of the motion will be an indirect censure of...Gupta, who has taken a tough line and told his party colleagues that he might quit if his writ as home minister cannot run," the Indian Express said on Friday.
Deve Gowda's aides have accused the media of exaggerating his standoff with Gupta.
"Why are you creating trouble?" Deve Gowda told reporters angrily on Thursday when he was asked to comment on his talks with Gupta over the Uttar Pradesh affair.
Uttar Pradesh sends 85 lawmakers to parliament, the biggest contingent from any state to the the 545-member lower house.
The BJP, which regards the state as its launching pad to federal power, was ruling Uttar Pradesh when a Hindu mob tore down a 16th century mosque in the town of Ayodhya in December 1992.
Some 3,000 people were killed in Hindu-Moslem clashes triggered by the demolition, forcing the government of then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to dismiss the BJP administration.
Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav, a staunch pro-Bhandari politician, wants Deve Gowda to continue with direct rule in Uttar Pradesh, preferably under the present governor.

Analysts said Deve Gowda wants Yadav to return to his former job as chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, possibly after another round of state elections, to tighten the United Front's hold on the politically crucial state.
